name: Old Persian
confidence_why: Kent 1950, Meillet 1915, Meillet and Benveniste 1931 and Schmitt 2004 all state that the Old Persian cuneiform inscriptions give no evidence for the place or nature of the accent beyond the existence of enclitics, and Skjaervo 2016 offers only a hedged comparative reconstruction (stress on the rightmost non-final heavy syllable) while saying outright that the rules are not known, so the classification that Old Persian stress is undetermined is the clear consensus.

catalog_locator: Kent 1950 sec. 59(i), p. 25 (chapter Phonology); Skjaervo 2016 p. 18
catalog_quote: Kent 1950 sec. 59(i): "There is no evidence as to the position and nature of the syllabic accent of OP, except that the presence of enclitic words shows that there was an accent." ... Skjaervo 2016 p. 18: "We do not know the rules for Old Persian stress, but some rules may be formulated from comparison with other Iranian languages and Indic. In words of two, three, or four syllables, the heavy syllable closest to the end of the word, not counting the last syllable, probably took the stress. Here “heavy syllable” = a syllable with a long vowel or a diphthong or a short vowel followed by more than one consonant (or an unwritten n or h + cons.) and “light syllable” = syllable with a short vowel followed by only one consonant ... We have no way of knowing whether words with a closed final syllable (= a final syllable with a final consonant) could be stressed on the last syllable ... In word…

audit.reasoning: Both deciding quotations were found verbatim at the stated locators in copies we hold (Kent 1950 sec. 59(i) p. 25; Skjaervo 2016 p. 18). The classification 'undetermined' rests on the standard reference grammar of a dead corpus language whose script does not mark accent, and is independently confirmed by every other description opened: Schmitt 2004 sec. 3.4 (held), and Meillet 1915 sec. 173 / Meillet-Benveniste 1931 sec. 173 (downloaded now to. The record already correctly separates Kent's 'no evidence' from Skjaervo's hedged comparative conjecture (rightmost non-final heavy) and Schmitt's note that OP>MP final-syllable loss suggests a Latin-type fixed accent. No better source can exist in principle; the only improvement would be citing Skjaervo's conjecture from his 2009 Routledge chapter rather than the not-for-citation primer. Limitation: n

sources.citation: Meillet, Antoine & Emile Benveniste. 1931. Grammaire du vieux-perse. 2e edition entierement corrigee et augmentee. Paris: Champion. (archive.org item meillet-grammaire-du-vieux-perse, scanned text)
sources.quote: 'Une insuffisance commune aux inscriptions perses et au texte avestique ... : on n'y trouve rien qui puisse renseigner soit sur une conservation eventuelle du ton indo-iranien, soit sur la place d'un accent. ... Mais il est impossible de dire s'il subsistait des traces du ton, qu'il soit reste mobile comme en vedique, ou qu'il ait tendu a se fixer.'

sources.citation: Meillet, Antoine. 1915. Grammaire du vieux perse. Paris: Maisonneuve. (archive.org item grammaireduvieux00meiluoft, scanned text)
sources.quote: 'Il y a une insuffisance qui est commune aux inscriptions perses et au texte avestique : on n'y trouve rien qui puisse renseigner soit sur une conservation eventuelle du ton indo-iranien, soit sur la place d'un accent. ... Mais il est impossible de dire s'il subsistait des traces du ton mobile comme dans la langue vedique.' Sec. 172 adds the only sentence-phonetic datum is the existence of enclitics (same point as Kent).
